rules.N1: Numbers A Form number is an int (i64, or u64 per N2) or a float (finite f64). The type is part of the value and is kept across every boundary: a float with no fractional part stays a float (`10.0` is written `10.0` in canonical JSON, `10` is an int), and `-0.0` keeps its sign (N3 F6). Derivation: encoding must be injective and round-trip, `decode(encode(v)) == v`, because replay rebuilds state from D. Turning `10.0` into `10` at a boundary would decode as an int, changing the static type a later step sees and the bits of later float arithmetic, so no normalization is applied. RCE's static types make the int/float distinction visible to the programmer, and canonical JSON keeps it visible in D.
rules.N10: Absence `none` and a present `()` differ, exactly as the Form's null-versus-absent rule: an option field holding none is present.
rules.N11: Time is the logical clock only: `Tick` events and `after n` in `select`. No construct reads a wall clock.
rules.N2: Integer arithmetic is checked: overflow of the *static type's* range is `trap("overflow: V is outside T")` with V the exact result and T the static type (`i64` for an untyped literal), never a wrap. `/` truncates toward zero (`-7 / 2 = -3`); `%` has the sign of the dividend (`-3 % 2 = -1`). Division or remainder by zero is `trap("division by zero")`. Modular and clamped arithmetic are explicit methods, never the default: `a.wrapping_add(b)`, `wrapping_sub`, `wrapping_mul` give the result modulo 2^N mapped into the static type's range, and `saturating_add`, `saturating_sub`, `saturating_mul` clamp it to the range; neither traps. u64 and usize arithmetic uses the Form ops `uadd usub umul udiv urem` (draft 0.5), which compute the exact result and trap unless it lies in [0, 2^64); a value at or above 2^63 is carried as an unsigned Form int, so `18446744073709551615 - 1` is exact. Lean: `RCE/U64.lean`. `i64.MIN / -1` and `i64.MIN % -1` are `trap("overflow: 9223372036854775808 is outside i64")` (the quotient is out of range; Rust's `checked_rem`). Shifts: `x << n` and `x >> n` with n ≥ bit width or n < 0 are `trap("shift amount out of range")`; `>>` is arithmetic for signed and logical for unsigned types. Bitwise `& | ^ ~` act on the two's-complement representation of the static type.
rules.N3: Floats The rules below are derived from IEEE 754-2019 and from two requirements of the Form: replay must give the same bits on every target (T1), and δ must be total (S1). `tests/float_rules.rs` checks each rule on the interpreter; the parity set carries the vectors of `examples/57_float_vectors.rce` to every CI target. - **F1 Correct rounding.** f64 is IEEE binary64. `+ - * /` and `sqrt` are the standard's basic operations, correctly rounded with roundTiesToEven, the default rounding-direction attribute; so are the conversion of an integer (`as f64`) and of a decimal literal. A correctly rounded operation is a function of its operands' bits alone, so every conforming target gives the same result: this is the only property determinism needs, and no other rounding mode exists in RCE. - **F2 One rounding per operator, in source order.** Float addition and multiplication are not associative and `a * b + c` with one rounding differs from two roundings (vector `MulSub`: `0.1 * 10.0 - 1.0` is `0`, fused it is `5.551115123125783e-17`). Contraction to fused multiply-add, reassociation, excess precision and every other value-changing optimization the standard allows a language to permit are therefore not valid compilations (HC-14). A fused multiply-add is itself correctly rounded, so it may exist only as an explicit named operation; RCE has none yet. Adding one needs a correctly rounded implementation on every runtime (Rust `f64::mul_add`, Java `Math.fma`, exact rational rounding in Python and JavaScript). - **F3 Subnormals are preserved.** Gradual underflow is part of the binary64 format; flush-to-zero and denormals-are-zero modes are not IEEE operations and would make `x - y == 0` hold for `x != y`. A host never enables them (HC-13); vectors `Mul(5e-324, 3.0)` and `Mul(2.2250738585072014e-308, 0.5)` detect either mode. - **F4 Non-finite results trap (from totality).** A Form value must have a reflexive equality and a total order (6.2, N5, N6) and must encode as a JSON number for hashing (N1). NaN is unequal to itself under IEEE comparison, and an infinity is not a JSON number and reintroduces NaN through `inf - inf` and `0 * inf`; the largest subset of binary64 closed under these requirements is the finite values. δ is total as a function into values and traps, so an operation whose IEEE result is not finite (the standard's overflow, divideByZero and invalid exceptions) is `trap("non-finite float")`. The alternatives fail a law: admitting NaN under the standard's totalOrder makes `==` disagree with IEEE comparison and needs a canonical NaN for hashing; saturating to the largest finite value is not an IEEE result and breaks `x * 2.0 / 2.0 == x` without a signal. With the trap every value is finite and every result that does not trap is the IEEE result. `x / 0.0` and `sqrt` of a negative number trap. - **F5 NaN payloads are never observable.** By F4 no NaN becomes a value, so its sign, payload and quiet bit cannot reach state, output or a hash; the standard leaves payload propagation to the implementation, which is why this matters. An implementation tests for a non-finite result before any NaN escapes, and the trap text is the same for every NaN. A fabric or target that can produce NaN (GPU, NPU, WASM SIMD) canonicalizes or traps before a value reaches state (HC-13; `wasm_float.rs` rewrites NaN to the canonical positive NaN). - **F6 Signed zero is a distinct state.** `-0.0` arises by the standard's sign rules, which are exact, so every target produces it in the same places (vector `Mul(0.0, -1.0)`). It is observable: `as f32` keeps the sign and f32 `tostr` prints `-0`, and the sign decides later results through the same exact rules. The state hash must be injective on observable state (otherwise two states a program can tell apart share a log entry), so canonical JSON keeps the sign and a state holding `-0.0` hashes differently from one holding `0.0`; this is correct, not a defect. `-0.0 == 0.0` is true (IEEE comparison), and f64 `tostr` prints `0` for both. - **F7 Exception flags are not state.** Inexact and underflow raise nothing (F1 already fixes the result); overflow, divideByZero and invalid are the trap of F4. No program reads a flag. - **F8 Exact operations.** `floor`, `ceil` and `round` are the standard's roundToIntegral operations toward negative, toward positive and ties-away (`(2.5).round()` is `3`, `(-2.5).round()` is `-3`); `abs` clears the sign. `min` and `max` follow N5. None of these rounds. - **F9 Transcendentals are excluded.** IEEE 754-2019 recommends but does not require correctly rounded `exp`, `log`, `sin`, `pow` and the like, and platform math libraries differ in the last bit. RCE has none. One may be added only with a correctly rounded implementation in the CORE-MATH or CRlibm style (correct rounding proved, or checked exhaustively for binary32), carried by every runtime rather than taken from the platform library; until then device versions are output only or verified (HC-13). Canonical float text is the shortest round-trip digits; decimal notation for 1e-5 ≤ |x| < 1e16, else `d.ddde±N` with `+` on positive exponents (`1e+300`, `1.5e-7`). Canonical JSON (6.1) has one float form, `interp::float_json`, used for hashes and for every trace and log written as JSON, so a trace shows the bytes that were hashed: shortest round-trip digits, decimal with at least one fractional digit for 1e-4 ≤ |x| < 1e16 (`10.0`, `0.0001`), otherwise exponent form without `+` (`1e16`, `1e-5`, `5e-324`), and `-0.0` keeps its sign (`tests/traces.rs` pins these forms). **f32 (draft 0.5).** The Form ops `f32add f32sub f32mul f32div` round both operands to binary32, compute in binary64, and round the result to binary32 (round to nearest even). Binary64 has 53 ≥ 2·24 + 2 significand bits, so by Figueroa's theorem the result equals the correctly rounded binary32 result, and every target (Rust `f32`, Python `struct`, JavaScript `Math.fround`) gives the same bits. A result outside the binary32 range is `trap("non-finite float")`. `x as f32` (Form `tof32`) rounds once. Lean: `RCE/F32.lean`.
rules.N4: Mixed arithmetic does not exist in RCE (both operands of a binary operator have the same static type). `a as f64` converts an integer exactly when |a| ≤ 2^53 and otherwise rounds to nearest even; `x as iN` truncates toward zero and traps if the result is out of range or x is not finite.
rules.N5: min / max compare exactly on integers and by IEEE order on floats (total, since operands are finite); on a tie the receiver is returned.
rules.N6: Equality is structural value equality within one static type; `1 == 1.0` is a type error (the type is part of the value, N1). Float `==` is IEEE comparison, so `-0.0 == 0.0` although the two are distinct states (N3 F6).
rules.N7: Text is a sequence of Unicode scalar values compared by code point, stored as UTF-8. From draft 0.5, `len`, indexing and slicing count UTF-8 bytes (Form `blen`, `bget`, `bslice`): `s[i]` is a `u8`, and a slice whose ends are not character boundaries is `trap("not a char boundary")`. `for c in s` and `chars()` still go by character. Case mapping (`upper`, `lower`) and class tests (`isdigit`, `isalpha`, `isupper`, `islower`) are ASCII-only; other characters are unchanged / false. `strip`, `words` and `toint` treat as whitespace exactly the 25 code points of the White_Space property of Unicode 18.0.0: U+0009 to U+000D, U+0020, U+0085, U+00A0, U+1680, U+2000 to U+200A, U+2028, U+2029, U+202F, U+205F and U+3000 (`interp::WHITE_SPACE`). `isspace` is ASCII (space, \t, \n, \x0c, \r). **Unicode pin.** RCE pins Unicode 18.0.0 (https://www.unicode.org/versions/Unicode18.0.0/) and reads no Unicode table at run time: scalar values and UTF-8 do not change between versions, case and class operations are ASCII, and the one property used, White_Space, is enumerated above rather than taken from the toolchain. A newer Rust, Python, JavaScript or JVM therefore cannot change a result; `tests/unicode_pin.rs` checks the set and scans the runtimes for calls that would read the toolchain's tables. Moving the pin is a spec change that must leave the enumerated set unchanged or bump the draft.
rules.N8: Indexing The index `i` of `a[i]` and the ends of `a[i:j]` have type `usize` (W-TY-1 otherwise), so no index is negative. `a[i]` with i ≥ n is `trap("index i out of range")`. A slice end above n is `trap("slice index out of range")`, and i > j is `trap("slice bounds reversed")`; an omitted end is 0 or n. Indexing and slicing are total or trapping by one rule: an out-of-range position is never silently moved.
rules.N9: Limits A list or text built by any operation is at most SIZE_LIMIT = 1,000,000 elements (`trap("size limit")`). A value written to state is at most VALUE_LIMIT = 1,048,576 bytes of canonical JSON (`trap("value limit")`, the event is refused, the value is not recorded).

table.class: linear, map receiver (maps are ordered association lists)
linear, set receiver (sets are sorted lists without duplicates)

table.work: n · ⌈log₂ n⌉, with ⌈log₂ n⌉ = 0 for n ≤ 1

rules.W-CAP-1: A capability outside an event payload field or a parameter; `Guarded` outside a state field; an authority that is not a declared struct.
rules.W-CAP-2: A step that writes a `Guarded[τ, A]` field on an event without a `Cap[A]` field. (W-NAME-2 refuses a declaration named after a 5.16 type or context.)
rules.W-CT-1: Comptime code that calls a non-comptime-safe function or traps or exceeds fuel.
rules.W-CTX-1: Context text made other than by `C.lit` of a string literal or `C.encode`; joined with another context or plain text; carried by an event payload; an unknown context.
rules.W-DEV-1: A growable value (`List`, `Map`, `Set`, `text`, slice, channel, iterator) bound in a device region, or `emit`, `spawn`, send, `select`, `yield` or a foreign call inside one (5.13).
rules.W-EFF-1: `emit`, `spawn`, channel operations or `select` in a pure `fn`; reading another region's fields in a step; calling a foreign function anywhere but `fn main` or a task function.
rules.W-FFI-1: An `extern` declaration whose ABI is not `"C"`, that is comptime or generic, or whose parameter or result types break 5.11; or a foreign function's name used other than as the callee of a direct call.
rules.W-INT-1: An `example` or `check` that does not hold.
rules.W-ITER-1: An iterator function that is not pure or has an arrow body; `yield` outside an iterator function; an `iter τ` value used other than as a `for` operand or `.collect()` receiver (5.14).
rules.W-LEX-1: Not UTF-8, BOM, bare CR, or a tab character.
rules.W-LEX-3: A literal outside every possible type range, or an invalid `\u{}`.
rules.W-LIN-1: A linear value not consumed exactly once on every path, copied, moved inside a loop, or placed in a collection, field, payload, channel or iterator (5.12).
rules.W-LOOP-1: A `LOOP_LIMIT` declaration that is not `const LOOP_LIMIT: u64 = n` with a positive literal n (6.7).
rules.W-MATCH-2: an unreachable arm (subsumed by earlier unguarded arms).
rules.W-MOD-2: import cycle. The reference checker reports a private name reached through `use` as W-VIS-1, which is the same rule.
rules.W-MOD-3: An imported name that clashes with a declaration of the importing module or with a name imported from another module (imported names are not renamed).
rules.W-NAME-1: Unresolved name, or a name resolved in the wrong namespace.
rules.W-NAME-2: Duplicate declaration in one scope; shadowing a parameter, field or module-level name inside the same item.
rules.W-OWN-3: Storing, returning (except R-RET) or capturing a borrow.
rules.W-PAT-1: A binding pattern whose name equals a variant in scope.
rules.W-PLACE: Left side of an assignment or `op=` is not a mutable place.
rules.W-REC-1: A cycle in the call graph, including through trait methods after monomorphization, other than a cycle of plain functions (one function calling itself included) whose calls are done by layered summed measures, or each of whose cycles of calls passes through a function declared with `bound` (6.7); `par` or `for … par` in a function of a cycle with a bounded function; `bound` on an iterator, a foreign function or a trait signature.
rules.W-REF-1: A refined type (5.1) that is generic, refines a type other than an integer type, `text` or a collection, or whose predicate is outside the decidable fragment (a term other than `self`, `self.len()` or an integer literal, an operator other than a comparison, `and`, `or`, `not`, or a call other than a text character class).
rules.W-REG-1: A region-typed value escaping its `with arena` block.
rules.W-SAFE-1: The identifiers `unsafe`, `Rc`, `Arc`, `RefCell`, `transmute`, `static`: refused with "memory safety is by construction" (there are no escape hatches in RCE other than the `extern` boundary of 5.11).
rules.W-SEC-1: An operator or method on a secret other than `==`/`!=`; a secret in an emitted value, a channel, an error payload or a foreign call.
rules.W-SIMD-1: A lane-wise operator on arrays of different lengths, of an unfixed length, or with non-numeric lanes (5.1).
rules.W-SPAWN-1: Spawning with a borrow or region-typed argument.
rules.W-STATE-2: a field initializer that is not a comptime constant
rules.W-STATE-3: a field type that is not an owned data type.
rules.W-STEP-1: A `step` naming an undeclared region or matching an undeclared event.
rules.W-STEP-2: **Totality**: an event that no step and no actor handler can ever match.
rules.W-STEP-3: The arrow form on a region with more than one field.
rules.W-STEP-4: Within one region, two unguarded steps whose patterns overlap (the second is unreachable).
rules.W-SYN-1: Not in the language of section 3.
rules.W-TRAIT-1: An impl not matching its trait
rules.W-TRAIT-3: a type used with `==`, `!=`, an ordering operator or a generic bound without implementing the trait it needs.
rules.W-TY-1: Any typing rule of section 5 fails.
rules.W-TY-2: Nested option `τ??`; borrow of a borrow `&&τ`; `[τ]` not behind a borrow; a borrow, region type or `fn` type inside a data type.
rules.W-VER-1: A first-line `# rce-version:` declaration naming a version other than 0.5, 0.6, 0.7 or 0.8 (2.7).
rules.W-VIS-1: W-MOD-1 `use` of a private item; W-MOD-2 import cycle. The reference checker reports a private name reached through `use` as W-VIS-1, which is the same rule.

rules.W-ATOM-1: `spawn`, a receive, `select` or another wait inside `atomic`.
rules.W-ATOM-2: actors of one `atomic` on different nodes.
rules.W-BUD-1: `with budget n` runs the block with a cost budget n: every Form operation charges its cost (C.6.4) and the operation that takes the total past n is `trap("budget")`, at the same operation on every target. The cost table is the reference evaluator's (`interp` and `conc.rs`, `charge`), listed in C.6.4. W-TY-1 if n is not an integer. `with budget n Block else [as e] Else` makes exhaustion a value. Derivation. Totality (T2) asks every step to end in a value; a trap that refuses the event is an outcome of the step, not a value the program can act on. To act on it the program needs a point where the trap is caught, and the state at that point must be one that some sequential execution reaches at a well-defined place, or Else observes a state no specification of Block describes. The only such states are the entry of Block and its completion; the trap rules out completion, so a caught trap restores the entry state. Block is therefore atomic: all of its writes or none (the same law as T30 for `atomic`). Normative rules: - A `trap("budget")` raised while Block runs, by this budget or any enclosing one, is caught by the innermost enclosing budget that has an `else`. Every write Block made (locals, struct fields, state fields, `self`) is undone, then Else runs. - `as e` binds `e: Exhausted`, the builtin `struct Exhausted { limit: u64, used: u64 }`, where `limit` is n and `used` is the units this frame had spent before the operation that would have passed a limit. - Charges stay. Cost counts operations performed (C.6.1), so the units spent in Block remain on every enclosing budget. When the trap came from an outer budget, Else charges that budget, its next charge traps again, and the trap reaches the next budget out with an `else`, or refuses the event. - W-BUD-1: Block of a budget with an `else` holds an effect that a trap cannot undo (`emit`, channel operations, spawn, select, yield, lvar `put` or `freeze`), or returns, breaks or continues out of it. - A budget without `else` behaves as before: the trap refuses the event. The trap falls on the same operation on every target, so whether Else runs, and the value of `e`, are functions of the program and its inputs, and replay re-derives them. The emitters save every local the block writes at entry (struct fields and state fields are locals of the emitted step) and restore them on the trap. Checked by `spec/checker/tests/conc06_run.rs` (`budget_else_catches`, `budget_else_refuses_undoable_effects`), `emit_run.rs` (`budget_else_*`, reference against the Rust, Python and JavaScript runtimes) and `emit06b.rs` (`budget_else_is_atomic_on_every_target`, the limit swept across the block's cost on all four targets).
rules.W-CRDT-1: C.11.5 Merge. `impl Merge for T` declares a join. Its laws (associative, commutative, idempotent) are an admission obligation (W-CRDT-1, `conc::crdt_gate`), discharged by a certificate and never by sampling. `bottom()` is the initial state; the states an LVar can reach are the up-set of it, which the join preserves, so the laws on that up-set are the laws of the type. For a kind of nullary variants the gate evaluates every triple, which decides them (`MergeLaws.laws_of_enum`). Otherwise the gate reads the body of `merge` as a term over proven combinators (`conc::merge_certs`): per field, `max` or `min` on an integer, `or` or `and` on a bool, `union` or `inter` on a `Set[τ]`, `merge` on a `Map[k, v]` (pointwise, certified when the `Merge` of `v` is: an integer, a bool, a set, a map of such, or a type with a certified impl), or `.merge` of a field whose type has a certified impl (componentwise product); on a record of one integer field, a selection that keeps `o` when `o.k > self.k` and `self` otherwise (max, or min when the smaller side is kept); and lexicographic on an integer key: `self` when `self.k > o.k`, `o` when `o.k > self.k`, and otherwise the key with the other fields merged by the rules above. Each term is a `Cert` of `MergeCert.lean`, and `Cert.semi` turns every certificate into a proof of the three laws, so they compose by construction. The lexicographic rule needs its key to be a chain (a total order); without that it is not a join (`MergeCert.lex_needs_chain`), which is why the key must be an integer. Any other impl is refused, also a lawful one written differently (for example bitwise `|`), with a message naming the combinators; a search on a finite sample runs first and, when it finds a counterexample, the refusal names it. The built-in instances (integers under `max`, `bool` under `or`, sets and lists under union, maps pointwise, tuples and records componentwise, `none` as bottom) have the laws by `MergeLaws.lean`, up to the point left open there: that sorted lists without duplicates represent sets and maps canonically.
rules.W-DL-1: outside `fn main` or a task function.
rules.W-GRP-1: a group not directly inside a device region.
rules.W-GRP-2: `barrier` other than as a statement at the top level of a group body.
rules.W-GRP-3: a lane reads another lane's slot in the same phase, or lanes share a scalar written in the phase.
rules.W-INTR-1: C.11.12 Real time. `interrupt event E priority p` with p an integer literal in 0..=255 (W-INTR-1). `step ... deadline n` with n a positive integer literal in ticks, and `const TICK_NS: u64 = n` when declared (W-RT-1). TICK_NS only relates logical ticks to a nominal duration for reporting; no construct reads a wall clock (6.3 N11).
rules.W-LVAR-1: inside the branches of one `par`, or the body of a `for ... par`, a `freeze` while some branch may `put`, where a call to a function or method that puts to (or freezes) an LVar it did not create counts as a put (or a freeze). An LVar a branch creates with `lvar_new` and does not rebind is its own and does not count. The rule does not match the name of a put with the name of a freeze, so an alias, a parameter or a helper cannot hide a freeze.
rules.W-LVAR-2: an empty threshold list, or a list with two elements that are, or on some input can be, one below the other in the program's `Merge` (`conc::lvar_gate`). This is decided at admission when every element takes finitely many values: a constant, or `if c then a else b` over such, with every combination checked, since two thresholds where one is below the other are compatible for any top. A parameter whose declared type is finite (a kind of nullary variants, or `bool`) and which the body never rebinds ranges over every value of its type, so it is decided too; since every value of such a type is at or above its bottom, a list with such a parameter and another element is refused whenever the bottom is below that element. Where an element is not finite in this sense (a parameter of an unbounded type, a computed value), incompatibility depends on the input, and the check every `wait` makes against the top, with its trap, is the defined behaviour. Model: T29q, T29s, T29a; the rule table `conc::LVAR_RULES` ties each rule and trap to its Lean declaration (see T29s).
rules.W-NAME-2: also refuses two branches with one name.
rules.W-ND-1: outside `fn main` or a task function. `select` without `nondet` keeps the rotation rule of 6.8.
rules.W-NODE-1: a placed name that is not an actor, or an actor placed twice. `supervisor S strategy k` with k one of `one_for_one`, `one_for_all`, `rest_for_one` (W-SUP-1); each `child` must be an actor (W-SUP-2), and W-NAME-2 refuses a duplicate child. Run-time meaning (normative). A supervisor declaration is one static supervisor; it supervises every actor whose type is one of its children, so the set an actor belongs to is fixed by the program, not by spawn order. When a handler of such an actor refuses its message (a trap or a `fail`), the run log records `Refused(reason)`, then `Restart(child, instance, reason, tick t, k)`, where `instance` is the actor's id (6.6) and k counts this child's restarts in the window below. The strategy then resets the region of the failed actor (`one_for_one`), of every actor of the supervisor's child types (`one_for_all`), or of those whose child is declared at or after the failed one (`rest_for_one`), to the actor's initializers. Intensity is measured in logical ticks, never wall time: with `const RESTART_WINDOW: u64 = W` only restarts at ticks t' with t - t' < W count, otherwise every restart of the run counts; more than the child's `restart bound` stops the supervisor with `Stopped(supervisor S)` and the run ends `Refused`. Mailbox policy: a restarted actor keeps its mailbox, since Form law 3 drops no message; only the message that failed is consumed, and it is logged as refused. A handler that fails inside `atomic` (C.11.10) leaves every handler of the batch uncommitted (T30), and the failing actor is then supervised as above. Restart as input. Derivation. The state of a run is the fold of its log (T3). A restart changes actor state without a message, so it must be an entry of the log that the fold applies, or the state is not a function of the log. The decision is therefore an input of the run: at a crash the run records `RestartIn{tick, sup, child, id, reset, stop}` (`RunResult.restarts`), and a replay given these inputs (`RunCfg.restarts`) applies each logged decision at its crash without consulting the supervisor's policy. A log thus replays under the decisions it records even after the strategy, bound or `RESTART_WINDOW` in the source has changed (the resolver rule of Appendix D, applied to supervision). A replayed decision for another actor or supervisor than the one that crashed is `replay diverged`. Checked by `spec/checker/tests/conc06b_run.rs` (`supervisor_restarts_then_stops`, `restart_is_an_input_replay_consumes`: replay reproduces the log, logged decisions govern under a changed bound, an edited decision is applied as logged, a mismatched one diverges) and `emit_run.rs` `actor_refusals_match` (the Rust, Python and JavaScript runtimes take the same decisions as the reference, with and without a window; they record, but do not yet replay, restart inputs). The run log of `fn main` is not D: actors run by `rce run`, not by the host of Appendix E (HC-6).
rules.W-PAR-1: the footprints of two branches overlap (write/write or write/read), including through a `&mut self` method call.
rules.W-PAR-2: a branch has an effect other than its own writes (`emit`, channel operations, spawn, foreign calls), or returns, breaks or continues out of the `par`.
rules.W-PAR-3: the body writes a place other than as a reduction (`+= *= &= |= ^=` on a variable never read in the body) or as slot `[i]` of a range loop over `i`.
rules.W-PAR-4: the body has an effect, or returns, breaks or continues.
rules.W-RT-1: C.11.12 Real time. `interrupt event E priority p` with p an integer literal in 0..=255 (W-INTR-1). `step ... deadline n` with n a positive integer literal in ticks, and `const TICK_NS: u64 = n` when declared (W-RT-1). TICK_NS only relates logical ticks to a nominal duration for reporting; no construct reads a wall clock (6.3 N11).
rules.W-SCOPE-1: C.11.9 Structured spawn. `spawn f(...) -> h` gives a join handle. In a version 0.6 module a task function may spawn only inside `scope`; `fn main` is an implicit scope (W-SCOPE-1). A join handle cannot leave its scope (W-SCOPE-1). A 0.5 module keeps the rule of 5.8: any task function may spawn.
rules.W-SES-1: an operation not allowed by the protocol state, an unknown label, `offer()` not matched over its labels, a match that does not handle every label, or branches leaving the endpoint in different states.
rules.W-SES-2: an endpoint not at the end of its protocol when it goes out of scope or is closed.
rules.W-SES-3: a label that appears twice, a protocol loop with no message before it repeats, or `break` outside a protocol loop.
rules.W-SUP-1: C.11.11 Placement and supervision. `node N {A, B}` places actors on a node. W-NODE-1: a placed name that is not an actor, or an actor placed twice. `supervisor S strategy k` with k one of `one_for_one`, `one_for_all`, `rest_for_one` (W-SUP-1); each `child` must be an actor (W-SUP-2), and W-NAME-2 refuses a duplicate child. Run-time meaning (normative). A supervisor declaration is one static supervisor; it supervises every actor whose type is one of its children, so the set an actor belongs to is fixed by the program, not by spawn order. When a handler of such an actor refuses its message (a trap or a `fail`), the run log records `Refused(reason)`, then `Restart(child, instance, reason, tick t, k)`, where `instance` is the actor's id (6.6) and k counts this child's restarts in the window below. The strategy then resets the region of the failed actor (`one_for_one`), of every actor of the supervisor's child types (`one_for_all`), or of those whose child is declared at or after the failed one (`rest_for_one`), to the actor's initializers. Intensity is measured in logical ticks, never wall time: with `const RESTART_WINDOW: u64 = W` only restarts at ticks t' with t - t' < W count, otherwise every restart of the run counts; more than the child's `restart bound` stops the supervisor with `Stopped(supervisor S)` and the run ends `Refused`. Mailbox policy: a restarted actor keeps its mailbox, since Form law 3 drops no message; only the message that failed is consumed, and it is logged as refused. A handler that fails inside `atomic` (C.11.10) leaves every handler of the batch uncommitted (T30), and the failing actor is then supervised as above. Restart as input. Derivation. The state of a run is the fold of its log (T3). A restart changes actor state without a message, so it must be an entry of the log that the fold applies, or the state is not a function of the log. The decision is therefore an input of the run: at a crash the run records `RestartIn{tick, sup, child, id, reset, stop}` (`RunResult.restarts`), and a replay given these inputs (`RunCfg.restarts`) applies each logged decision at its crash without consulting the supervisor's policy. A log thus replays under the decisions it records even after the strategy, bound or `RESTART_WINDOW` in the source has changed (the resolver rule of Appendix D, applied to supervision). A replayed decision for another actor or supervisor than the one that crashed is `replay diverged`. Checked by `spec/checker/tests/conc06b_run.rs` (`supervisor_restarts_then_stops`, `restart_is_an_input_replay_consumes`: replay reproduces the log, logged decisions govern under a changed bound, an edited decision is applied as logged, a mismatched one diverges) and `emit_run.rs` `actor_refusals_match` (the Rust, Python and JavaScript runtimes take the same decisions as the reference, with and without a window; they record, but do not yet replay, restart inputs). The run log of `fn main` is not D: actors run by `rce run`, not by the host of Appendix E (HC-6).

rules.W-TY-1: if n is not an integer. `with budget n Block else [as e] Else` makes exhaustion a value. Derivation. Totality (T2) asks every step to end in a value; a trap that refuses the event is an outcome of the step, not a value the program can act on. To act on it the program needs a point where the trap is caught, and the state at that point must be one that some sequential execution reaches at a well-defined place, or Else observes a state no specification of Block describes. The only such states are the entry of Block and its completion; the trap rules out completion, so a caught trap restores the entry state. Block is therefore atomic: all of its writes or none (the same law as T30 for `atomic`). Normative rules: - A `trap("budget")` raised while Block runs, by this budget or any enclosing one, is caught by the innermost enclosing budget that has an `else`. Every write Block made (locals, struct fields, state fields, `self`) is undone, then Else runs. - `as e` binds `e: Exhausted`, the builtin `struct Exhausted { limit: u64, used: u64 }`, where `limit` is n and `used` is the units this frame had spent before the operation that would have passed a limit. - Charges stay. Cost counts operations performed (C.6.1), so the units spent in Block remain on every enclosing budget. When the trap came from an outer budget, Else charges that budget, its next charge traps again, and the trap reaches the next budget out with an `else`, or refuses the event. - W-BUD-1: Block of a budget with an `else` holds an effect that a trap cannot undo (`emit`, channel operations, spawn, select, yield, lvar `put` or `freeze`), or returns, breaks or continues out of it. - A budget without `else` behaves as before: the trap refuses the event. The trap falls on the same operation on every target, so whether Else runs, and the value of `e`, are functions of the program and its inputs, and replay re-derives them. The emitters save every local the block writes at entry (struct fields and state fields are locals of the emitted step) and restore them on the trap. Checked by `spec/checker/tests/conc06_run.rs` (`budget_else_catches`, `budget_else_refuses_undoable_effects`), `emit_run.rs` (`budget_else_*`, reference against the Rust, Python and JavaScript runtimes) and `emit06b.rs` (`budget_else_is_atomic_on_every_target`, the limit swept across the block's cost on all four targets).
